lessons.title: mein, dein, sein, ihr — possessive articles
lessons.summary: One set of endings covers my, your, his, her, our and their — the exact same endings ein and kein already use.
lessons.rule:
A possessive is the little word that says who something belongs to: my bag, your car, her brother. Turkish glues this onto the noun as a suffix — çanta-m — but German puts a separate word in front of the noun, in the very same slot where der or ein would go. So you say meine Tasche, never die meine Tasche. One slot, one word.

Here is the good news, and it really is the whole lesson: possessives take exactly the same endings as ein and kein. If you can already say einen Bruder, then you can say meinen Bruder, deinen Bruder, seinen Bruder, unseren Bruder. Eight words, one pattern.

Think of every possessive as two pieces stuck together. The front piece says whose it is and follows the owner: mein-, dein-, sein-, ihr-. The ending ignores the owner completely — it reacts only to the noun that comes next: is that noun a der, die or das word, and what job is it doing in the sentence? German calls those jobs cases:

  • Nominative — the doer of the sentence: Mein Bruder kommt.
  • Accusative — the thing the action lands on: Ich suche meinen Bruder.
  • Dative — the receiver, and whatever follows mit, bei, zu: Ich fahre mit meinem Bruder.

So in Anna sucht ihren Bruder, ihr- is there because Anna is female, and -en is there because der Bruder is masculine and is the thing being searched for. The two halves have nothing to do with each other.

Two of these words are famously confusing. sein means his — and also its. ihr means her — and also their. And Ihr with a capital I in the middle of a sentence means your, when you address someone politely as Sie. Only that capital letter separates the last two, so write it carefully in emails and forms. One spelling wrinkle too: euer (your, to several friends) drops its second e as soon as an ending appears — euer Auto but eure Wohnung, euren Bruder. Nobody says eueren.

tables.title: ein, kein, mein, ihr — identical endings

examples.note: Bruder is masculine and it is the doer here, so no ending at all — exactly like ein Bruder.
Same word, different job: the key is what I'm looking for, so masculine takes -en.
die Tasche is feminine, so the ending is -e — like eine Tasche.

examples.de: Das ist Anna. Ihr Mann heißt Tom.
examples.en: That's Anna. Her husband is called Tom.
examples.note: Anna is the owner, so the stem is ihr-. Mann is masculine and the doer, so no ending.
mit always forces the dative, and neuter dative is -em.
Capital I = polite 'your'. With a small i, ihre would mean her or their.

mistakes.why: der Schlüssel is masculine and it is the thing being searched for, so the ending is -en — the same -en you already use in einen Schlüssel.

mistakes.wrong: Das ist Anna. Seine Tasche ist neu.
mistakes.right: Das ist Anna. Ihre Tasche ist neu.
mistakes.why: The front piece follows the owner, not the noun. Anna is female, so it is ihr-; sein- would say the bag belongs to a man.
Masculine in the nominative takes no ending at all. -e is not a default; it belongs to feminine and plural.

mistakes.wrong: Wie ist ihre Adresse, Herr Schmidt?
mistakes.right: Wie ist Ihre Adresse, Herr Schmidt?
mistakes.why: When you say Sie to someone, their 'your' is written with a capital I. Lowercase ihre means her or their and reads as a different person.

drills.question: Das ist ___ Bruder. (my)
drills.explain: Bruder is masculine and is the doer of the sentence, and masculine doers take no ending — just like ein Bruder.

drills.question: Wo ist ___ Tasche? (your — to a friend)
drills.explain: die Tasche is feminine, and feminine always adds -e, exactly like eine Tasche.

drills.question: Ich suche ___ Schlüssel. (my)
drills.explain: The key is the thing the action lands on, and masculine is the only gender that visibly changes there: -en.

drills.question: Das ist Anna. ___ Mann heißt Tom.
drills.explain: The owner is Anna, so the stem must be ihr-, and masculine Mann as the doer adds nothing.

drills.question: Wie ist ___ Telefonnummer, Frau Meier?
drills.explain: You are using Sie with Frau Meier, and the polite 'your' is written with a capital I.

drills.question: Er fährt mit ___ Auto. (his)
drills.explain: mit always pushes the next word into the dative, and neuter dative ends in -em.
Plural takes -e, and the conjugated verb still has to be the second element of the sentence.

drills.answer: Ich gebe meiner Schwester einen Apfel
drills.explain: The sister receives, so feminine dative -er; the apple is what gets handed over, so masculine -en.

lessons.title: The verb goes second — always
lessons.summary: In a German statement the conjugated verb is the second element, no matter what you put first — and the subject moves behind it.
lessons.rule:
If you learn one structural rule in German, learn this one: in a normal statement the conjugated verb sits in position 2. "Conjugated" just means the form that has changed to match the person doing it — ich gehe, du gehst, wir gehen. Position 2 means: exactly one thing stands before it, then the verb.

And position 2 counts chunks of meaning, not words. Everything in front of the verb has to be one single unit — one idea. Ich is a chunk. Morgen is a chunk. Morgen früh um sechs Uhr is still one chunk, because it is one piece of information about time. Whatever you choose, only that one chunk is allowed in front of the verb.

Now the consequence that feels strange at first. If you put something other than the subject in front — a time word, a place, a linking word — the subject does not disappear. It jumps behind the verb. Ich gehe heute ins Kino. becomes Heute gehe ich ins Kino. Never Heute ich gehe... That is the loudest foreign-accent mistake in German, and it is exactly what English and Turkish word order push you towards.

Germans front things constantly, because position 1 is where you put whatever the sentence is really about, or whatever links it to the sentence before: Dann fahre ich nach Hause. Deshalb lerne ich Deutsch. In Berlin ist das normal. The verb itself never moves — everything else rearranges around it.

Two footnotes. The glue words und, aber, oder, denn sit outside the sentence, so they do not fill position 1: Aber ich habe keine Zeit. is correct. And this rule describes main clauses — a piece that could stand alone as a complete sentence. Words like weil and dass build a different kind of clause that kicks the verb all the way to the end, which is its own lesson.

tables.title: Same sentence, five ways in — the verb never moves
Where the verb goes, by sentence type

examples.note: The plain version: subject in position 1, verb in position 2.
heute took position 1, so ich had to move behind the verb. Same meaning, more natural in a conversation about today.

examples.de: Am Wochenende fahren wir nach Hamburg.
examples.en: At the weekend we're going to Hamburg.
examples.note: Am Wochenende is two words but one chunk, so it fills position 1 by itself.
Linking words like deshalb take position 1 themselves — the subject follows the verb.

examples.en: Tomorrow I have to get up early.
examples.note: With two verbs only the conjugated one (muss) is in position 2; aufstehen waits at the very end.
aber is glue between sentences, not position 1 — so the normal order simply continues.

mistakes.why: Only one chunk may stand before the verb. Once heute has that spot, ich has to move behind gehe.
The same trap with a modal verb: the conjugated piece is muss, and that is what belongs in position 2.

mistakes.wrong: Ich jeden Tag fahre mit dem Bus.
mistakes.right: Ich fahre jeden Tag mit dem Bus.
mistakes.why: Nothing is allowed to squeeze in between position 1 and the verb. Time expressions go after the verb, not before it.
This is over-applying the rule. und, aber, oder and denn sit outside the sentence, so they never occupy position 1.

drills.question: Which sentence is correct?
drills.explain: heute already fills position 1, so the verb must come straight after it and the subject drops in behind.

drills.question: Morgen ___ nach Hamburg.
drills.explain: After a fronted time word the verb comes immediately, and the subject follows it.

drills.question: Am Montag ___ ich zu Hause. (arbeiten)
drills.explain: The verb takes position 2 right after the time chunk, and it still has to match ich.

drills.question: Rewrite with heute first — Ich habe heute Zeit. → Heute ___ ich Zeit.
drills.explain: Fronting heute pushes the subject behind the verb, but the verb form itself does not change.

drills.question: Aber ___ heute keine Zeit.
drills.explain: aber is glue between sentences and does not fill position 1, so the normal subject-then-verb order stays.

drills.answer: Am Wochenende fahren wir nach Hamburg
drills.explain: Am Wochenende is a single chunk in position 1, so the verb is next and wir comes after it.

drills.answer: Meine Frau und ich wohnen in Berlin
drills.explain: Four words, but one chunk — the subject — so the verb is still counted as the second element.
Only the conjugated verb muss takes position 2; the unchanged aufstehen is parked at the end.

lessons.title: Asking questions
lessons.summary: Two shapes only: verb first for yes/no questions, question word first for everything else — plus the wo / wohin / woher split.
lessons.rule:
German asks questions in exactly two shapes, and neither one needs a helper word. English sticks do in front — Do you live here? German has nothing like that. You simply move the verb.

Shape 1 — yes/no questions. Take the statement and put the conjugated verb right at the front. "Conjugated" means the form that changed to match the person: ich wohne, du wohnst, er wohnt. So Du wohnst hier. becomes Wohnst du hier? The subject follows immediately after it.

Shape 2 — W-questions. Start with the question word (nearly all of them begin with w), then the verb, then the subject: Wo wohnst du? Wann kommt der Zug? This is not a new rule at all — the W-word is simply filling position 1, and the verb is still the second element, exactly as in a statement.

The part that trips up every English speaker is wo / wohin / woher. English uses where for all three. German splits them, and here Turkish helps you far more than English does: wo = nerede, wohin = nereye, woher = nereden. If the verb involves movement (gehen, fahren, kommen), you almost certainly need wohin or woher, not wo.

Answering: ja for yes, nein for no — and doch, which English has no word for. Use doch to contradict a negative question: Kommst du nicht mit? — Doch! meaning "Yes, I actually am coming."

tables.title: Three kinds of "where"
rows: a place you are — Wo bist du?

tables.title: The two shapes next to a statement

examples.note: Verb at the front = yes/no question. Nothing else is added.
English needs 'do'; German just moves hast to the front.
Question word, then verb, then subject — the verb is still the second element.
Origin → woher (nereden). Probably the first question a new neighbour will ask you.
The bus is moving, so it is a direction → wohin (nereye), never wo.
wie viel is one chunk in position 1, so kostet comes straight after it.

mistakes.why: gehen is movement, so German needs the direction word wohin (Turkish nereye). wo only asks about a fixed place.
kommen points back at an origin, so the question word must be woher (nereden).
The verb comes immediately after the question word. German never leaves the subject sitting between the two.
German asks 'how' is your name, not 'what'. In everyday speech people just say Wie heißt du?

drills.question: ___ wohnst du?
drills.explain: wohnen is about the place you are, not a direction — Turkish nerede.

drills.question: ___ kommst du? — Aus der Türkei.
drills.explain: The answer names an origin, and origins are asked with woher — Turkish nereden.

drills.question: ___ fährt dieser Bus?
drills.explain: The bus is going somewhere, and a direction always takes wohin — Turkish nereye.

drills.question: ___ du Zeit? (haben)
drills.explain: A yes/no question starts with the conjugated verb, and haben with du becomes hast.

drills.question: Which sentence is correct?
drills.explain: After the question word the verb comes next and the subject after it — nothing may sit in between.

drills.question: ___ kostet das Ticket? (how much)
drills.explain: wie viel asks about an amount, and it counts as the single chunk in position 1.
Question word first, verb second, subject last — the same position-2 rule as in a statement.
There is no question word here, so the verb itself starts the sentence — that is what makes it a yes/no question.
